<p>I know it was a bit mouthful to describe but because of these reasons, I think it’s totally worth making it! 😉 It’s crunchy and moreish and perfect as a <a href="https://mykoreankitchen.com/12-korean-foods-that-will-impress-your-party-guests/">party</a> appetiser.</p><div id="AdThrive_Content_1_desktop" class="adthrive-ad adthrive-sticky-container adthrive-content adthrive-content-1 adthrive-ad-cls"></div>
<p>I used to eat it a lot after school on my way home. The street vendor I used to go to served it in a paper cup and they gave me a toothpick to eat it with, so it was very easy and convenient to eat while walking home.</p>
<p>I don’t know who invented this Korean style popcorn chicken and when, but I want to say to whoever you are, it’s BRILLIANT!</p>

<h2>Korean Popcorn Chicken (Dakgangjeong, 닭강정) vs. Korean Fried Chicken (Yangnyeom Tongdak, 양념통닭)</h2>
<p>You might be wondering what’s the difference between Korean popcorn chicken and Korean fried chicken? Frankly, I don’t think there’s much difference. In fact, some Koreans use these two names interchangeably.</p>
<p>However, as the name suggests, the popcorn chicken is bite-sized fried chicken and is typically made with boneless chicken fillets. (I prefer thigh over breast as it’s more moist.)</p>
<p>On the other hand, Korean fried chicken is typically made with larger chunks of  any chicken cuts. It usually includes bone-in chicken but you can also make them with boneless chicken as well.</p><div id="AdThrive_Content_2_desktop" class="adthrive-ad adthrive-sticky-container adthrive-content adthrive-content-2 adthrive-ad-cls"></div>
<p>Also, I find that Korean popcorn chicken are more tender and sweeter, less spicy and less garlicky.</p>

<p>However, all these facts will be dependent on the cook’s choice in ingredients.  Therefore, these two may result in the same outcome depending on who’s cooking it and how. 😉</p>
<p>I personally prefer Korean popcorn chicken over typical Korean fried chicken because it’s easier and more neat to eat.</p>
<p>Anyway, I hope you show some Korean popcorn chicken love this weekend! I’m sure your family and friends will appreciate this!</p>

Ingredients for Korean Popcorn Chicken (2 to 3 servings)</strong></h3>
<h4>Main</h4><div id="AdThrive_Content_4_desktop" class="adthrive-ad adthrive-sticky-container adthrive-content adthrive-content-4 adthrive-ad-cls"></div>
<ul>
<li>500g/ 18 ounces chicken thigh fillets (or breast fillets), rinsed under cold water, cut into bite sized pieces</li>
<li>150g/ 5.3 ounces fresh <a href="http://amzn.to/1WDCckv" rel="nofollow">Korean rice cake</a>, cut in half (If you’re not using fresh rice cakes, separate and soak them in warm water for 10 minutes before cutting. Pat them dry with paper towels to remove any moisture.)</li>
<li>1 Tbsp <a href="http://amzn.to/1OCwWWn" rel="nofollow">rice wine</a></li>
<li>2 tsp ginger powder</li>
<li>1/2 tsp fine sea salt</li>
<li>1/4 tsp ground black pepper</li>
<li>1 cup <a href="http://amzn.to/1sv2OHO" rel="nofollow">potato starch</a> or corn starch</li>
<li>Some cooking oil for deep frying (I used <a href="http://amzn.to/20cKvSA" rel="nofollow">rice bran oil</a>)</li>
</ul>
<h4>Sauce (mix these in a bowl)</h4>
<ul>
<li>5 Tbsp tomato sauce/ketchup</li>
<li>1 & 1/2 Tbsp <a href="http://amzn.to/1sv2VTD" rel="nofollow">gochujang</a> (Korean chilli paste)</li>
<li>2 Tbsp honey</li>
<li>2 Tbsp dark brown sugar</li>
<li>1 Tbsp <a href="http://amzn.to/1OCxoEf" rel="nofollow">soy sauce</a></li>
<li>2 tsp <a href="http://amzn.to/20cLhiq" rel="nofollow">sesame oil</a></li>
<li>1/2 tsp minced garlic</li>
</ul><div id="AdThrive_Content_5_desktop" class="adthrive-ad adthrive-sticky-container adthrive-content adthrive-content-5 adthrive-ad-cls"></div>
<h4>Optional – to garnish</h4>
<ul>
<li>Crushed nuts or <a href="http://amzn.to/1TqIW1t" rel="nofollow">seeds</a> (e.g. walnut, peanut, pistachio, sunflower seeds and sesame seeds, etc.)</li>
<li>Finely chopped green onion – if you want the nice colour contrast</li>
</ul>
<p>*1 Tbsp = 15 ml, 1 Cup = 250 ml</p>
<p>**If you want to learn more about Korean ingredients, check my <a href="https://mykoreankitchen.com/essential-korean-cooking-ingredients/">essential Korean cooking ingredients</a>!</p>
<h3><strong>How to Make Korean Popcorn Chicken</strong></h3>
<p>1. Place chicken pieces into a large mixing bowl. Add the rice wine, ginger powder, salt, and ground black pepper and mix them well. Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and marinate the chicken for 30 mins in the fridge.</p>

<p> </p><div id="AdThrive_Content_6_desktop" class="adthrive-ad adthrive-sticky-container adthrive-content adthrive-content-6 adthrive-ad-cls"></div>
<p>2. Coat each chicken piece with the starch powder thoroughly. (It’s best doing this in 4 to 5 batches so that they are well covered with the starch powder.)</p>

<p>3. Pour some cooking oil into a deep saucepan/wok and heat until it reaches 175 C/ 347 F (or boiling).</p><div id="AdThrive_Content_7_desktop" class="adthrive-ad adthrive-sticky-container adthrive-content adthrive-content-7 adthrive-ad-cls"></div>
<p>Deep fry the rice cakes in batches until the outer layer turns crispy. (Deep-frying for too long can lead to rice cake explosions, so cook for less than 10 seconds. Alternatively, you can lightly pan fry them until soft.) Take them out and set aside onto paper towel to absorb any excess oil. Repeat this with the remaining rice cakes.</p>
<p>Deep fry the battered chicken pieces in batches until golden and cooked through (2 to 3 mins). Take them out and set aside onto paper towel to absorb any excess oil. Repeat this with the remaining chicken. (Don’t put too much chicken in one go as it can lower the oil temperature too much.) To make the chicken extra crunchy, double fry them one more time. Set aside.</p>
<p><div class="dpsp-pin-it-wrapper aligncenter size-full wp-image-8261 perfmatters-lazy dpsp-always-show-mobile dpsp-always-show-desktop"><img decoding="async" class="" src="data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='650'%20height='650'%20viewBox='0%200%20650%20650'%3E%3C/svg%3E" alt="Korean style popcorn chicken deep frying" width="650" height="650" data-pin-media="https://mykoreankitchen.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/Korean-style-popcorn-chicken-deep-frying.jpg" data-src="https://mykoreankitchen.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/Korean-style-popcorn-chicken-deep-frying.jpg" data-srcset="https://mykoreankitchen.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/Korean-style-popcorn-chicken-deep-frying.jpg 650w, https://mykoreankitchen.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/Korean-style-popcorn-chicken-deep-frying-300x300.jpg 300w, https://mykoreankitchen.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/Korean-style-popcorn-chicken-deep-frying-500x500.jpg 500w, https://mykoreankitchen.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/Korean-style-popcorn-chicken-deep-frying-150x150.jpg 150w" data-sizes="(max-width: 650px) 100vw, 650px" data-pin-description="Korean Style Popcorn Chicken" data-pin-title="Korean Style Popcorn Chicken"><span class="dpsp-pin-it-overlay"></span><a class="dpsp-pin-it-button dpsp-pin-it-button-top-right dpsp-pin-it-button-shape-rounded" target="_blank" rel="noopener" style="--dpsp-pin-background: #c92228; <p>4. Pour the sauce into a heated skillet. Bring it to boil on medium heat until the sauce thickens a little bit (1 to 2 mins). Stir constantly. Add the fried chicken and rice cakes then coat with the sauce quickly and thoroughly. Garnish with your choice of toppings (e.g. crushed nuts, seeds and green onion). Serve.</p>

<h3><strong>Tips</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>If you can’t find the Korean rice cakes, it’s OK to leave these out. I included them here because that’s how a Korean street food stall or a restaurant serves these popcorn chicken. If you’re leaving these rice cakes out, maybe add more chicken to match up with the sauce quantity.</li>
<li>It tastes best when served immediately after cooking. (The crunchiness of chicken is at its peak then.) However, it can be served cold as well. Any leftover meat can be refrigerated in an airtight container for the next day. It might not be as crispy as the first day but it still tastes really good!</li>
<li>For a little bit of variety, you can set aside some un-sauced double fried popcorn chicken and serve them like that. As the chicken is marinated with ginger powder, salt and black pepper during the initial process, it has a really nice taste on its own. People who can’t eat spicy food really appreciate this!</li>
</ul><div id="AdThrive_Content_9_desktop" class="adthrive-ad adthrive-sticky-container adthrive-content adthrive-content-9 adthrive-ad-cls"></div>

Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and marinate the chicken for 30 mins in the fridge.</div></li><li id="wprm-recipe-9213-step-0-1" class="wprm-recipe-instruction" style="list-style-type: none;"><div class="wprm-recipe-instruction-text" style="margin-bottom: 5px;">Coat each chicken piece with the starch powder thoroughly. (It’s best doing this in 4 to 5 batches so that they are well covered with the starch powder.)</div></li><li id="wprm-recipe-9213-step-0-2" class="wprm-recipe-instruction" style="list-style-type: none;"><div class="wprm-recipe-instruction-text" style="margin-bottom: 5px;"><span style="display: block;">- Pour some cooking oil into a deep saucepan/wok and heat until it reaches 175 C/ 347 F (or boiling).  </span><div class="wprm-spacer"></div><span style="display: block;">- Deep fry the rice cakes in batches until the outer layer turns crispy. (Deep-frying for too long can lead to rice cake explosions, so cook for less than 10 seconds. Alternatively, you can lightly pan fry them until soft.) Take them out and set aside onto paper towel to absorb any excess oil. Repeat this with the remaining rice cakes. </span><div class="wprm-spacer"></div><span style="display: block;">- Deep fry the battered chicken pieces in batches until golden and cooked through (2 to 3 mins). Take them out and set aside onto paper towel to absorb any excess oil. Repeat this with the remaining chicken. (Don’t put too much chicken in one go as it can lower the oil temperature down.) To make the chicken extra crunchy, double fry them one more time. Set aside.</span></div></li><div id="AdThrive_Recipe_2_desktop" class="adthrive-ad adthrive-recipe adthrive-recipe-1 adthrive-ad-cls" style="min-height: 250px;"></div><li id="wprm-recipe-9213-step-0-3" class="wprm-recipe-instruction" style="list-style-type: none;"><div class="wprm-recipe-instruction-text" style="margin-bottom: 5px;"><span style="display: block;">Pour the sauce into a heated skillet. Garnish with your choice of toppings (e.g. crushed nuts, seeds and green onion). Serve.</span></div></li></ul></div></div>

<p>Delicious – But BEWARE THE RICE CAKE EXPLOSION!!!!</p>
<p>This recipe was great. Chicken was cripsy and delicious, and I loved the sauce (I did add a tablespoon of rice vinegar to temper the sweetness a bit). </p>
<p>Why the 4 instead of a 5? The line “under 30 seconds to avoid possible rice cake explosion” is an understatement and needs to be emphasized in bold and all caps. YOU DO NOT WANT A RICE CAKE EXPLOSION, IT WILL HAPPEN QUICKLY AND WITHOUT WARNING, IT MIGHT NOT EVEN TAKE 30 SECONDS, AND IT WILL BE DANGEROUS AND MESSY. The morning after, I’m still cleaning oil off of my kitchen, and I have a couple of nice red marks on my hands. Next time, I might do these in smaller batches or in a fry basket so I can more quickly remove them from the oil.</p>
